details: Global nuclear power capacity (April 2026): ~415 GWe total installed; ~440 operating reactors (IAEA PRIS); countries with nuclear power: 32 nations; largest programs: USA (93 reactors; ~100 GWe); France (56 reactors; ~62 GWe); China (55+ reactors; ~55 GWe; fastest growth); Russia (37 reactors; ~28 GWe); South Korea (25 reactors; ~24 GWe); India (22 reactors; ~7 GWe); Japan (12 operating of 33 total; post-Fukushima restarts ongoing); Ukraine (15 reactors; ~14 GWe); reactor types operating: PWR (most common ~70%); BWR (~15%); PHWR/CANDU (~8%); RBMK (~3%; Russia only); other (<5%)
chernobyl_impact: Pre-Chernobyl (1985): ~370 GWe operating; ~560 reactors under construction globally; after Chernobyl 1986-2000: new reactor orders essentially stopped in USA (last US order before Chernobyl cancelled post-accident); construction programs slowed; 10 reactors cancelled in Germany; after Fukushima 2011: Germany committed to phase-out (completed 2023); Switzerland phase-out started; Japan shut all 54 reactors then restarting gradually; China continued building (unaffected by Western public opinion shift); Net effect: Chernobyl + Fukushima delayed nuclear expansion by ~20-30yr in Western countries; gap to be filled by renewables debate; see reactor_types_physics_comparison_REAL.csv for design comparison

details: Nuclear power operational safety statistics (OECD NEA): occupational radiation doses: collective dose per unit electricity: ~3 person-mSv/GWe-yr (worldwide average 2015-2020 operating reactors); individual worker dose: typical annual 1-3 mSv/yr for most workers; industrial accident rate (conventional safety): nuclear power = one of safest industries for worker safety per kWh; WANO performance indicator: collective radiation exposure declining 30-50% from 1991 to 2020 (improved shielding; work planning; dose management; robot-assisted maintenance); fatal accident rate (industrial): nuclear ~0.03 deaths/TWh (including Chernobyl+Fukushima direct deaths); coal: 2.8 deaths/TWh (air pollution + industrial accidents)
chernobyl_impact: Deaths per TWh comparison (lifecycle including accidents; WHO estimates): coal = 2.8; oil = 1.8; natural gas = 0.3; hydro = 0.04; wind = 0.04; nuclear = 0.03; solar = 0.02; nuclear safety reputation vs statistical reality: nuclear is among safest per unit energy despite two INES-7 accidents; Chernobyl-specific: ~56 confirmed direct deaths (UNSCEAR 2008; UN Chernobyl Forum); +~4000-6000 projected eventual cancer deaths in 600,000 liquidators; but: displacement-related deaths ~30,000-50,000 excess over lifetime from psychosocial harm; economic disruption death burden>>radiation death burden; 'deaths from nuclear' critically depends on what you count
source: NEA 2022; Ritchie 2020 Our World in Data; WHO 2006; UNSCEAR 2008; stochastic_deterministic_effects_REAL.csv

details: Nuclear power levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) 2026: new nuclear (Gen-III; AP1000/EPR): $80-200/MWh (large range reflecting construction cost risk); existing nuclear (operating cost only): $30-40/MWh (most competitive electricity source); solar PV (utility): $25-50/MWh; wind (onshore): $25-50/MWh; CCGT (natural gas): $60-100/MWh; coal: $65-150/MWh; nuclear: HIGH capital cost but LOW fuel + operating cost; fuel cost = ~5% of LCOE (vs 60-80% for gas); decommissioning: adds $3-10/MWh (amortized); waste disposal: adds $1-5/MWh; Chernobyl costs: sarcophagus + NSC + decommissioning + social benefits = estimated $200-700B total
chernobyl_impact: Chernobyl economic impact on nuclear industry: insurance cost increased dramatically post-1986; all nuclear plants required to fund decommissioning from operations; waste disposal fees mandatory; public opposition → licensing delays → increased capital costs; Price-Anderson Act (USA): industry liability capped at $12.6B; government covers losses above; justification: no private insurance possible for INES-7 event; post-Fukushima: German nuclear phase-out = additional €50B decommissioning costs; low-carbon value of nuclear: offsetting CO₂ emissions: nuclear avoids ~2.5 billion tonnes CO₂/year globally (at 415 GWe × 90% capacity × 8760hr × 0.8 kgCO₂/kWh coal equivalent)
source: chernobyl_economic_impact_REAL.csv; NEA 2023 Projected Costs; IPCC AR6; World Nuclear Association

details: Current RBMK operation (2026): 11 RBMK-1000 reactors operating in Russia: Leningrad NPP (4 units); Smolensk NPP (3 units); Kursk NPP (4 units; 2 original + 2 upgraded); all modified post-1986: graphite tip problem solved; ORM increased from 15 to 30 rods minimum; enrichment 2.8% → 2.8% + Pu recycle; SCRAM time reduced 18s → 12s; positive void coefficient: reduced from +4-8 pcm/%void to +0.5-2 pcm/%void (additional absorbers added); still positive but no longer capable of 1986-type excursion at modified operating conditions; IAEA Safety Assessment 2010: modified RBMK acceptable for continued operation with enhanced monitoring; WANO peer reviews ongoing; no RBMK incidents since 1986
chernobyl_impact: RBMK operational lifetime: Leningrad 1 (commissioned 1974) extended to 2040 = 66yr license; first nuclear plant to exceed 50yr operation; economic justification: fully amortized → very low operating cost; Russia: nuclear = 19% electricity (2024); RBMK units are significant baseload; decommissioning RBMK: complex (graphite moderator = radioactive C-14; difficult to classify/dispose); Russia has no completed RBMK decommissioning example; Chernobyl Units 1-3 (RBMK) = first RBMK decommissioning attempt; 2064 target; rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv has full modification details
source: rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv; IAEA PRIS; World Nuclear Association; reactor_types_physics_comparison_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl impact on public perception of nuclear power: polling data (Eurobarometer; Gallup): before Chernobyl 1985: 50-60% of European public supportive of nuclear; after Chernobyl 1986: dropped to 30-40%; after Fukushima 2011: dropped further to 20-35% in Europe; Germany: 70-80% anti-nuclear post-Fukushima (phase-out completed 2023); France: 40% pro-nuclear (most nuclear-dependent large country); USA: stable ~50% support; China: less public polling but government = strongly pro-nuclear (60 GWe build pipeline); media: Chernobyl = most referenced nuclear event in journalism; HBO 2019 miniseries: won Emmy; 100M+ viewers; renewed public awareness; historical irony: HBO series = most accurate dramatic portrayal of nuclear accident = net positive for nuclear literacy despite anti-nuclear cultural background
chernobyl_impact: Chernobyl effect on nuclear attitudes: longitudinal polling shows: (1) immediate sharp drop after accident; (2) gradual recovery 1990-2010; (3) second drop after Fukushima; (4) current gradual recovery linked to climate change concerns and energy security (Ukraine war 2022 + gas price spike → nuclear viewed more favorably in Europe); climate change framing: nuclear = low-carbon; coal = high-carbon; choice becomes: accept nuclear risk vs accept climate risk; 2022-2025: nuclear seen as energy security asset in Europe (vs Russian gas dependence); Finland, France, UK building new reactors; UK: SMR (Small Modular Reactor) program active

details: Generation IV reactor inherent safety features: NRC/IAEA Generation IV designation = reactors with significantly improved safety; key safety improvements: (1) Passive cooling: no pumps required for decay heat removal; relies on natural convection (e.g., AP1000 gravity-feed tanks; passive recirculation); eliminates Fukushima-class station blackout as risk; (2) Negative void coefficient: PWR/VVER/BWR all have negative void coefficient; void formation → reduced reactivity → self-limiting; (3) Lower power density: some SMRs; (4) Integral design: integral PWR (iPWR) = all primary components inside pressure vessel → no large-break LOCA possible; (5) Sub-atmospheric pressure: molten salt reactors → no high-pressure radioactive coolant to drive dispersion
chernobyl_impact: RBMK-1000 had: positive void coefficient; no containment; no passive cooling → 3 safety deficiencies each of which was individually sufficient to make accident worse; Gen-IV: all 3 addressed; inherent safety argument: RBMK was NOT inherently safe (relied on operator compliance with ORM rules that were poorly understood and monitored); Gen-IV reactor physics self-limits power; inherent = if ALL active systems fail AND operators do nothing: reactor remains safe; Example: AP1000 passive cooling: 3-day passive cooling from gravity tanks; no operator action required for 72hr; TMI required active operator intervention to prevent worse; Chernobyl operators' actions = made things worse; inherent safety removes operator-accident coupling
source: reactor_types_physics_comparison_REAL.csv; IAEA GIF Gen-IV International Forum; AP1000 DCD; ukraine_nuclear_fleet_REAL.csv

details: Small Modular Reactors (SMRs): IAEA definition: <300 MWe per unit; modular = factory-built; transportable; many designs under development 2026: NuScale VOYGR (77 MWe; USA; first licensed SMR globally 2022; cancelled project 2023 due to cost); Rolls-Royce SMR (470 MWe; UK; pre-licensing 2026); GE-Hitachi BWRX-300 (300 MWe; Canada/Poland licensing); Rosatom RITM-200 (55 MWe; floating; operating on Akademik Lomonosov since 2019); X-energy Xe-100 (80 MWe; HTGR; USA DOE grant); TerraPower Natrium (345 MWe; sodium fast; Wyoming 2028 target); Ukraine interest: SMRs for areas near CEZ as energy source; Energoatom/Westinghouse AP300 MOU 2022
chernobyl_impact: SMR safety case: factory manufacturing = quality control vs site construction; smaller unit = lower radioactive inventory per reactor; passive safety standard; siting flexibility (underground; smaller EPZ); Ukraine war context: distributed SMRs less vulnerable than large centralized NPPs; Chernobyl demonstrated: large centralized reactor failure → national-scale consequence; SMR failure (if containment works): local consequence only; IAEA SMR regulatory framework: developing 2022-2028; NuScale cancellation 2023: showed SMR economics challenging at small scale vs large plant; cost per kWh = currently higher for SMR than large LWR; learning curve expected to reduce costs in 2030s
source: reactor_types_physics_comparison_REAL.csv; NuScale regulatory review; IAEA SMR technology assessment 2022; ukraine_nuclear_fleet_REAL.csv

details: Permanent nuclear waste disposal: Onkalo facility (Finland; POSIVA): world's first permanent repository for high-level spent fuel approved for operation; located at 400m depth in crystalline bedrock (Precambrian; 1.9 billion yr old granite); opened for waste emplacement 2025 (first containers); design: copper canister (5 cm thick) inside bentonite clay buffer inside granite rock; multi-barrier system: copper 100,000yr corrosion resistance; bentonite 1M yr swelling capacity; granite stable for geological time; capacity: all Finnish spent fuel (~6,500 tonnes HM); operational: 2025-2150 (filling phase); sealing: ~2150-2200; isolation: permanent; other countries: Sweden Forsmark (site selected; construction approval 2022); Finland/Sweden = only operational/approved repositories globally
chernobyl_impact: Chernobyl spent fuel (21,217 assemblies in ISF-2): no permanent repository plan for Ukraine; ISF-2 = interim storage (100yr design); Ukraine does not have a geological repository; feasibility studies exist for crystalline rock in western Ukraine; timeline: 2064 decommissioning → ISF-2 holds fuel; eventually → deep geological repository needed; cost: €10-30B estimated; funding = unresolved; international approaches: multinational repository concept (EU discussion); Ukraine potential candidate given large spent fuel inventory; war has interrupted repository planning; Chernobyl's 21,217 assemblies = one major input; Units 1-3 decommissioning fuel = additional; total Ukrainian spent fuel inventory ~2060: ~40,000 tonnes HM
source: chernobyl_decommissioning_physics_REAL.csv; chernobyl_spent_fuel_isf2_REAL.csv; IAEA Nuclear Waste Safety Standards; POSIVA Oy
